title: Why enzymes hit a speed limit

scenes.visual: Toll booth analogy: cars arrive at a booth at low, medium, and high traffic; throughput rises then caps; EZPass raises the cap.
scenes.narration: Think of an enzyme like a toll booth. When traffic is light, low substrate, every car gets processed as fast as it arrives, so velocity is proportional to substrate. When substrate equals Km, you're at half capacity. And when traffic is heavy, high substrate, the booth is saturated, working flat out at Vmax. Adding more cars doesn't make the worker any faster. Saturation doesn't mean the enzyme stops. It means it's already going as fast as it possibly can.
scenes.notes: Adding more cars doesn't make the toll-booth worker faster once they're at capacity — and EZPass is what changes the Vmax of toll collection. Saturation doesn't mean the enzyme stops working; it's working at maximum capacity. Once every active site is occupied, adding more substrate can't push velocity past Vmax.

scenes.visual: Michaelis-Menten curve drawn from the equation; regions highlighted: linear, diminishing returns, plateau at Vmax = kcat[E]; Km marked at half Vmax.
scenes.narration: This curve is the Rosetta Stone of enzyme kinetics. Almost every idea you'll meet maps onto it. At low substrate concentration, the rate rises nearly linearly, and the enzyme's performance depends on kcat over Km. Push higher, and you hit diminishing returns. At high substrate, the enzyme is saturated. Adding more barely changes the rate, and you're at Vmax, which equals kcat times the enzyme concentration. Km sits at the midpoint of the curve, where velocity is half of Vmax. Read it as how much substrate the enzyme needs to get going, not automatically as a measure of affinity.
scenes.notes: This curve is the Rosetta Stone of enzyme kinetics — almost every idea maps onto it. At low [S] the rate rises nearly linearly and performance depends on kcat/Km; push higher and you hit diminishing returns; at high [S] the enzyme is saturated (Vmax = kcat·[E]), where adding more substrate barely changes the rate. Km sits at the midpoint, where v = ½Vmax — read it as "how much substrate the enzyme needs," not automatically as affinity.

scenes.visual: Three curves with Km 0.5, 2, 5 mM sharing one Vmax; lowest Km reaches half-max soonest.
scenes.narration: Here's what makes Km so useful. An enzyme can prefer one substrate over another. The one with the lowest Km is captured most efficiently, reaching half-maximal speed at the lowest concentration. It's like a vending machine that takes quarters, dimes, and pennies. Same output, but it handles quarters most smoothly. And remarkably, an enzyme's Km is usually close to the substrate concentration it actually sees inside the living cell.
scenes.notes: An enzyme can "prefer" certain substrates — the one with the lowest Km is captured most efficiently. It's like a vending machine that takes quarters, dimes, and pennies: same output, but it processes quarters most smoothly. A small Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at low substrate — and Km is roughly the substrate concentration the enzyme actually sees in vivo.

scenes.visual: kcat = Vmax/[E]T; log scale from lysozyme 0.5/s to carbonic anhydrase 600,000/s.
scenes.narration: Vmax depends on how much enzyme you added. So to describe the enzyme molecule itself, we use kcat, the turnover number. It's the number of reactions one enzyme molecule can run per second when it's fully saturated. It's top speed. Carbonic anhydrase clocks an astonishing 600,000 per second. Lysozyme plods along at about one reaction every two seconds. But kcat is only top speed. It doesn't tell you how the enzyme performs when substrate is scarce. For that, you want kcat over Km, the catalytic efficiency.
scenes.slideTitle: Turnover Number: the enzyme's speed limit (kcat)
scenes.notes: kcat tells you how many reactions one enzyme molecule can catalyze per second when fully saturated — its speed limit. Carbonic anhydrase runs at ~600,000 per second; lysozyme is a plodding ~0.5 per second. kcat = Vmax/[E]ᴛ divides out how much enzyme you added, giving a property of the molecule itself. It is top speed, though — it doesn't tell you how the enzyme does when substrate is rare (that's kcat/Km).
